  In compliance with the Americans with Disability Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this
  meeting, please contact the City Clerk’s Office (310) 510-0220, Notification 48 hours prior to the meeting will
  enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting. (28 CFR 35. 102-
  35,104 ADA Title Il). All public records relating to an agenda item on this agenda are available for the public
  inspection at the time the records are distributed to all, or a majority of all, members of the City Council. Such
  records shall be available at City Hall located at 410 Avalon Canyon Rd.

Due to social distancing recommendations from the Center for Disease Control and State of
California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA) and the County of Los
Angeles, and pursuant to findings made under AB 361, the CITY OF AVALON’S CITY COUNCIL
SHALL GENERALLY BE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC REMOTELY. The general public may
attend the meeting in the Council Chambers however must adhere to social distancing
requirements. The public is encouraged to watch and participate from the safety of their homes
while practicing social distancing.

Council Chambers are open to the general public. Once the Council Chambers reach maximum
occupancy (as determined by the Fire Chief), the general public may participate in Oral
Communication and address the City Council on an agenda item in person by waiting in the City
Hall Court Yard and entering the Chambers one at a time at the appropriate time. No one will be
admitted into the Council Chambers who is ill or exhibiting symptoms of COVID-19. Additionally,
the general public may participate in Oral Communication and address the City Council on an
agenda items by providing comments via Zoom or by sending comments to
askcityofavalon.com.

  For the public’s convenience, but not participation, the meeting can be viewed:

3.  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote Teleconferencef\Jirtual City Council Meetings
  Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361
  As the State of Emergency has ended, the City Council can continue to hold virtual
  meetings without providing notice of the City Council’s teleconference location if the City
  Council makes the following two findings: (1) State or local officials have imposed or
  recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19; and
  (2) The City Council reconsiders the circumstances of the state of the emergency and
  danger presented by COVID-19; Having made the findings, the City Council can continue
  every 30 days to authorize meetings under AB 261 to protect the health or safety of
  attendees.
  Recommended Action
  Reconsider the circumstances of COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed by the
  Governor and COVID-19’s continued impact and determine that state or local officials
  have imposed or recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with
  COVID-19, and as such, that continuing to utilize the protections of Assembly Bill 361 will
  protect the health and safely of attendees.

4.  Fiscal Year 2023-2024 First Quarter Treasurer’s Report
  State and Municipal Codes require the Treasurer to submit within 30 days following each
  fiscal quarter a report summarizing the City’s cash and investment balances. Attached is
  the First Quarter Treasurer’s Report for FY23-24. The report was shared with the City
  Treasurer prior to presentation to City Council.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt a resolution accepting the FY23-24 First Quarter Treasurer’s Report.

5.  Avalon Kids Baseball Lease
  Avalon Kids Baseball, a local non-profit organization that manages the local little league,
  request a lease for an 8 foot by 20-foot plastic storage shed. The shed will be positioned
  between the bathrooms and dugout on the southeasterly portion of the bricked area at
  JMF. Staff recommend the City Council authorize the City Manager to enter into a lease
  agreement with Avalon Kids Baseball for the proposed 160 square foot storage space for
  $1 per year as is consistent with the City’s treatment of other non-profit lessees.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to enter into a lease agreement with Avalon Kids Baseball to
  store a storage shed at Joe Machado Field.

6.  Adopt an Ordinance Amending Title 6, Chapter 6-1, Section 6-1.128, Animal Care, of the
  Avalon Municipal Code and Adoption of Exemption Findings Under the California
  Environmental Quality Act
  This ordinance was introduced and all further readings were waived during the November
  2, 2023 Special City Council Meeting. Members of the City requested an amendment to
  the Avalon Municipal Code to more specifically address, strengthen protections, and
  prohibit hunting, trapping, feeding, luring, inhumane treatment, and killing of wild animals
  — including deer within the City of Avalon.
  —

  Recommended Action
  Adopt an ordinance of the City of Avalon amending Title 6, Chapter 6-1, Section 6-1.128
  Animal Care of the Avalon Municipal Code and Adoption of Exemption Findings Under
  the California Environmental Quality Act.

7.  Declaration of Surplus Property “Southwesterly 2 Feet” of Tremont Avenue
  —

  During a Closed Session of the May 16, 2023 City Council Meeting, the Council
  considered real property negotiations regarding a portion of the public right of way located
  along Tremont Street. Staff has determined that access/control of the property and
  establishing security can be accomplished through the sale of the parcel back to the
  adjacent property owner and placement of a restriction on the deed that no building can
  be built on the parcel.
  Recommended Action
  (1) Adopt a resolution declaring the approximate 102 square foot area of land identified
  as the ‘southwesterly 2 feet” on sheet 4 of 11 of the City’s Encroachment Survey as
  surplus; and (2) Authorize the City Manager or his designee to sell the property, in
  accordance with the City’s policy, to the adjacent landowners Cow Hoyt and George
  —

  Paquette.

GENERAL BUSINESS

8.  2023 Community Survey Report
  In June, City Council awarded a contract with Zilo International to conduct a Community
  Survey via mail, online, and in-person following stringent US Department of Housing and
  Urban Development CDBG income survey questions and guidelines. In August and
  September 2023 Zilo International received a total of 635 surveys and in October
  consulted with City staff to validate 451.
  Recommended Action
  Receive and file the 2023 Community Income Survey Report

9.  First Reading of an Ordinance Amending Title 3, Chapter 3-1, Section 3-1.116 Revocation
  or Suspension of Licenses of the Avalon Municipal Code
  The proposed ordinance revision will expand grounds for business license suspension or
  revocation to include non-compliance with any local, state or federal regulation.
  Recommended Action
  Introduce and waive the all further readings of an ordinance of the City of Avalon
  amending Title 3. Chapter 3-1, Section 3-1.116 Revocation or Suspension of Licenses of
  the Avalon Municipal Code.

10.  Avalon Destinations LLC Transportation Permit Application
  On October 21, 2023, Shari Cobb of Avalon Destinations LLC submitted a Transportation
  Permit application to provide transportation between transient rental customers
  arrival/departure location (Cabrillo Mole, Heliport, Green Pier) to one of four Avalon
  Destinations LLC vacation rentals.
  Recommended Action
  Discuss and provide direction to Staff. If consensus to approve is reached, make the
  affirmative finding that the criteria set forth in Avalon Municipal Code Section 5-14.04 has
  been meet.

11.  ICON of Avalon Transportation Permit Application
  On September 27, 2023, the City received a transportation permit from Scott Gorelczenko
  on behalf of ICON of Avalon. On October 3, 2023, the transportation permit application
  was presented to City Council during the regularly scheduled meeting. After discussion
  and concerns over increasing the amount of vehicles on roadways, the applicant is
  proposing an amendment to the initial application.
  Recommended Action
  Discuss and provide direction to Staff. If consensus for approval is reached, make the
  affirmative findings that the criteria set forth in Avalon Municipal Code Section 5-11 have
  been met and direct Staff to issue the appropriate permit.

12.  Avalon Wastewater Treatment Plant Soffit Repair and Chlorine Tank Replacement
  Procurement
  The City’s wastewater treatment plant operator, PERC Water Corporation, is completing
  major infrastructure repairs throughout the City’s Waste Water Treatment Plant
 CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
NOVEMBER 7, 2023
PAGE 5

  (WWTP).Two projects of significance include the repair and replacement of a soffit
  located in the facility’s basement and the rehabilitation of the V’JWTP’s chlorine contact
  tank
  Recommended Action
  (1) Make the affirmative finding that the City will not gain a competitive advantage by
  using the formal contract bid or other competitive procedure as outlined by the Avalon
  Municipal Code Section 3-4.111(c); (2) Authorize the procurement of supplies, equipment
  and services for the replacement and repair of the WWTP soffit for a not to exceed sum
  of $65,000; and 3. Authorize the procurement of supplies, equipment and services for the
  replacement and repair of the WWTP chlorine tank for a not to exceed sum of S145000.

13.  Authorize the Solicitation of a Request for Bids for the Five Corner Pedestrian
  Improvements Proiect
  Since 2018, work has proceeded on developing the construction contract documents to
  implement the reconstruction of the five corners intersection including the roadway
  segments of Tremont Avenue and Avalon Canyon Road in the near vicinity of the
  intersection. The project proposes to construct new permanent sidewalks, median safety
  islands, traffic calming and lighting in order to provide safer operations for all users.
  Recommended Action
  (1) Authorize the solicitation of a request for bids for the construction contract for the Five
  Corner Intersection Enhancement and Safety Improvement Project. (2) Approve the
  design and construction plans of the project. (3) Authorizes the City Manager or his
  designee to modify plans as needed for compliance with funding agencies.

SUBJECT:  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote Teleconference/Virtual City
  Council Meetings Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Reconsider the circumstances of CCVID-1 9 state of emergency
proclaimed by the Governor and CCVI D-19’s continued impact and determine that state or local
officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection
with COVID-19, and as such, that continuing to utilize the protections of Assembly Bill 361 will
protect the health and safely of attendees.

REPORT SUMMARY: Traditionally, the Brown Act allows for teleconference or virtual meetings.
provided that the physical locations of the legislative body’s members joining by teleconference
are posted on the agenda, that those locations are open to the public and that a quorum of the
members is located within its jurisdiction. AS 361 provides an exception to these procedures in
order to allow for fully virtual meetings during proclaimed emergencies, including the COVID-19
pandemic.

Since March of 2020 and the issuance of Governor Newsom’s Executive Order N-29-20, which
suspended portions of the Brown Act relating to teleconferencing, the City Council has had virtual
meetings without having to post the location of the legislative body members attending virtually.
Most public agencies have been holding public meetings using virtual platforms since this time.
In June of 2021, Governor Newsom issued Executive Order N-08-21, which provided that the
exceptions contained in EO N-29-20 would sunset on September 30. 2021.

On September 10, 2021, the Legislature adopted AB 361, which allows public agencies to hold
fully virtual meetings under certain circumstances without the posting of the agenda from each
location a legislative body member is attending. Governor Newsom signed the bill into law on
September 16,2021. Because it contained an urgency provision, it took immediate effect.

Specific Findings Required under AS 361

As the State of Emergency has ended, the City Council can continue to hold virtual meetings
without providing notice of the City Council’s teleconference location if the City Council makes
the following two findings:

  1. State or local officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social
  distancing in connection with COVID-19; and

  2. The City Council reconsiders the circumstances of the state of the emergency and danger
  presented by CCVID-19;

 Having made the findings, the City Council can continue every 30 days to authorize meetings

  Additionally, Cal/OHSA has implemented COVI D-1 9 Prevention Non-Emergency Regulations
that will remain in effect until February 3, 2025. The City’s economy is dependent upon visitors

having members of the public attend council meetings at locations where council members are
in attendance due to their desire to avoid exposure to COVID-19 poses a risk to the health or
safety of attendees.

Re-Authorization is Required Within 30 Days

The City Council made the required findings at its October 17, 2023 City Council meeting.
Consistent with the provisions of AB 361, the new findings must be made every 30 days. Thus,
if the City Council desires to continue to meet remotely without having to post the location of each
teleconference location, the City Council reconsider the facts of the state of emergency and
continued impact of COVID-19, find that state or local officials have imposed or recommended
measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and therefore, that remote
meetings under AB 361 should continue in order to protect the health or safety of attendees.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City Council will
have to follow the Brown Act provisions that existed prior to the COVID-1 9 pandemic.

28, 2023 City Council meeting.

SUBJECT:  Fiscal Year 2023-2024 First Quarter Treasurer’s Report

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt a resolution accepting the FY23-24 First Quarter
Treasurer’s Report.

REPORT SUMMARY: State and Municipal Codes require the Treasurer to submit within
30 days following each fiscal quarter a report summarizing the City’s cash and investment
balances. Attached is the First Quarter Treasurer’s Report for FY23-24. The report was shared
with the City Treasurer prior to presentation to City Council.

The purpose of the report is to inform, on a quarterly basis, the City’s cash and investment
balances, the investment types, yields, and market values, and to ensure that the City’s
investments are in compliance with the City’s adopted investment policy. The report shows that
all of the City’s funds are in compliance with its investment policy. In general, operating cash is
held in US Bank checking accounts and any excess cash is invested in California’s Local
Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) and various certificates of deposit (CD5). In accordance with
Government Code sections 16429.1 and 53601 et seq., the City cannot invest more than 30%
of its portfolio in CDs. CDs accounted for 17.3% of the unrestricted cash and investments for
the quarter ended September 30, 2023. On July 26, 2023, the City purchased $5125 million of
United State Treasury Bills maturing on January 25, 2024 with a yield to maturity of 5.265%
using funds previously held in LAIF. The investment will yield the City approximately $50,000
in additional investment income over the six month period compared to holding the funds in
LAIF over the same period. The City will continue to assess for opportunities to increase its
investment returns while maintaining necessary liquidity and compliance with its investment
policy.

The unrestricted cash balance for the first quarter of 2023-2024 totaled $23.27 million, an
increase of $2.11 million from the fourth quarter of 2022-2023. The unrestricted cash balance
includes cash from enterprise funds (e.g. Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste) not available for
general government functions. The increase in unrestricted cash is attributable to the
seasonality of visitor-driven tax revenues and the timing of significant capital outlays
anticipated to increase during the second and third quarter of the fiscal year. The unrestricted
cash balance increased by $4.62 million compared to the first quarter of 2022-2023. The
increase in unrestricted cash balance from the prior fiscal year is attributable to visitor-driven
tax revenues and fees again significantly exceeding pre-COVID revenues, as well as due to
the timing of significant capital outlays. The City expects to begin construction on several major
 capital projects, including the second phase of the Cabrillo Mole Ferry Terminal rehabilitation
and the Five Corners Pedestrian Improvement project, during the fiscal year which will reduce
future unrestricted cash balances.

Chapter 6-1, Section 6-1.128 Animal Care of the Avalon Municipal Code and Adoption of
Exemption Findings Under the California Environmental Quality Act.

REPORT SUMMARY: This ordinance was introduced and all further readings were waived
during the November 2, 2023 Special City Council Meeting.

This item appeared on the November 2, 2023 Special City Council Meeting agenda at the
collective request of the City Council. The requested changes were incorporated into the first
reading of the ordinance and are contained in the ordinance to be adopted. At the November
2, 2023, meeting, the importance of the health, safety and welfare of City residents and visitors
was discusses and many public comments in support of the ordinance were received.

During the October 17, 2023 regular City Council Meeting, the City Council heard a public
presentation from the Catalina Island Conservancy regarding the planned Catalina Island
Restoration Project. During the same meeting, Council heard approximately two hours of public
comments from 28 different speakers regarding the proposed Restoration Project and,
specifically, the planned eradication of the island’s deer population the majority spoke against
  —

the project.

After thoughtful consideration, members of the City Council contacted City Staff and the City
Attorney’s office to request an amendment to the Avalon Municipal Code to more specifically
address, strengthen protections, and prohibit hunting, trapping, feeding, luring, inhumane
treatment, and killing of wild animals including deer within the City of Avalon.
  —  —

In revising and clarifying the Municipal Code, the City Council makes the determination that
hunting, pursuing, feeding, killing, or trapping animals within the City represents a threat to public
health, safety, and welfare to the residents and visitors within the City of Avalon. Additionally,
City Council makes the determination that the feeding, luring, pursuing, or trapping of wild
animals for the purposes of capturing and/or killing such wild animals can be cruel and abusive
to such animals and inconsistent with the residential, recreational, and visitor-friendly nature of
the City. Feeding wildlife can lead to overpopulation, the spread of diseases, and altered natural
behaviors. Additionally, hunting and trapping within City boundaries poses significant safety risks
to residents and visitors, and raises a plethora of ethical and environmental concerns. Hunting
 and trapping within city limits could cause death, accidents, or harm to residents and visitors
alike, and ensures human safety. Trapped animals could harm residents and visitors, as
frightened animals can become aggressive in their attempts to escape. Frightened animals can
also move quickly and without warning, causing car or bike accidents, at times fatal. Even when
exercising the highest degree of care, hunting can pose a risk to residents and visitors of Avalon
as it is densely populated, and the use of firearms for hunting purposes is incompatible with this
densely-populated area. To address these issues, an ordinance disallowing the feeding,
trapping, pursuing, killing, and hunting of animals within city limits has been proposed.

The proposed ordinance establishes penalties for non-compliance including fines of up to $5,000
per occurrence.

The ordinance also provides exemptions for emergency action taken by trained authorized
personnel to euthanize an animal found severely injured within the City as well as exemptions
for trapping feral cats and dogs for the purpose of spayed or neutering. There is also an
exception for bird feeders located on private property.

ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW: The ordinance is not a project subject to the California
Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) pursuant to Section 15378 (the activity will not result in a
direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the environment) of the State CEQA
Guidelines, California Code of Regulations, Title 14, Chapter 3, because it has no potential for
resulting in physical change to the environment, directly or indirectly. Additionally, the ordinance
is exempt under CEQA pursuant to Guidelines Section 15061(b)(3) (there exists no possibility
that the activity will have a significant adverse effect on the environment) because this ordinance
will not cause a change in any of the physical conditions within the area affected by the
ordinance. No development would result from implementation of the ordinance. The ordinance
preserves the status quo and avoids the potential for accidents related to hunting and use of
firearms within a densely-populated area. The ordinance prohibits hunting within City limits, and
would not result in an increase in deer population, as it also prohibits feeding wildlife which could
lead to overpopulation. The ordinance avoids indirect impacts related to hunting within City limits
as the prohibition on hunting would avoid noise impacts, potential water quality impacts related
to bullets, and other health and safety impacts related to firearm-related accidents. The
ordinance does not result in any indirect impacts on the environment related to overpopulation
of wild animals, including mule deer, as it is strictly limited to City limits and hunting may continue
outside of the City.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Undetermined.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The Avalon Municipal
Code will not be amended.

Background
Nestled on Santa Catalina Island, Avalon is a unique city that holds the distinction of
being the only incorporated city on the island. This charming city is renowned for its
picturesque setting, combining natural beauty with a touch of coastal allure.

The population size can vary due to seasonal tourism and the fact that it is a resort
community, however it is estimated that there are about 3,460 residents.

The population ofAvalon is influenced by several factors, including the number of
residents who live there year-round, seasonal workers, and the influx of tourists,
especially during peak vacation times. The city’s population might experience
fluctuations, with more people during tourist seasons and potentially fewer during
off-peak times.
Avalon’s community is known for its close-knit atmosphere, and the residents often
engage in activities that reflect the island lifestyle.
The City of Avalon: Governance structure
Avalon’s municipal government follows the council—manager model. The Mayor is
elected for a two-year term, and City Council Members serve four-year terms. The City
Council directly appoints the City Manager, who acts as the city’s executive officer

 ENGAGEMENT PROCESS
 Zilo team collaborated closely with the City of Avalon to formulate survey questions and design
social media content and outreach strategies. Additionally, the City created a page on their
website to keep the community informed about ongoing activities and guide them to the
necessary resources for participation.
Various methods were employed to gather survey responses, encompassing online
submissions, mailed responses, and in-person interactions to help ensure a statistically
significant sample of Avalon’s population.

Survey Instrument

The survey followed CDBG guidelines and asked for the household’s approximate annual
income. Given the various participation methods, we included an address request to
safeguard against duplicate responses from the same household, enhancing the survey’s data
integrity. Additionally, obtaining addresses served the dual purpose of confirming the
respondent’s residency in Avalon, providing an added layer of authenticity to the collected
data. Our commitment to respondent privacy was paramount, and we communicated
transparently about how the data would be used, assuring participants that their information
wouldn’t be shared beyond the research team.

The survey covered various other aspects, including the number of residents in the household,
immediate family members residing together, homeownership or renting status, and whether
the residence is employer-subsidized. Additionally, we inquired about the duration of their
residency in Avalon, employment details, health coverage, internet access, transportation
modes, ferry frequency to the mainland, and demographic information.

To cater to a diverse audience, the survey was provided in both English and Spanish. Each
survey packet included a cover letter in both languages explaining the survey’s purpose,
English and Spanish versions of the two-page survey, and a stamped return envelope with the
address. For reference, samples of the survey documents can be found in Appendix A.

Survey Distribution
Surveys were mailed to reach every household with a PC Box on the island the week of
August 14th, 2023. Due to Avalon’s mail system limitations, where mail is not delivered to
street addresses, residents engaged in mail transactions are required to secure a post office
box. Each survey package included Spanish and English translations, along with a stamped
return envelope. The accompanying cover letter included information about the survey and
provided a link to the online survey and a QR code for those who preferred internet-based

A grand total of 635 surveys were gathered, with 204 received via mail, 161 submitted online,
and 270 conducted through door-to-door efforts. Among these, 65 were in Spanish, and 570
were in English.

Acknowledging the notable presence of second homes and short-term rentals with temporary
occupants in Avalon, these units were purposely omitted from the survey. The main objective
was to collect information about permanent residents. Respondents who identified as living in
Avalon for less than four months annually were also not included in the overall report results.
To be deemed valid, surveys needed both a valid address and income information.

Every survey underwent validation and was subsequently included in the final tabulations. Out
of these, 451 surveys were deemed valid and incorporated in this report.
The overall survey results have a precision of +1-3.26% margin of error at the 99% confidence
level, based on the population size of 3460 and 1074 individual represented in the 451 valid
surveys. We can conclude that the results of this survey accurately represents the community.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Introduce and waive the all further readings of an ordinance of
the City of Avalon amending Title 3, Chapter 3-1, Section 3-1.116 Revocation or Suspension of
Licenses of the Avalon Municipal Code.

REPORT SUMMARY: City Staff recommend amending Title 3, Chapter 3-1. Section 3-1116
Revocation or Suspension of Licenses of the Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) to broaden potential
revocable or suspension violations to include noncompliance with any local, state or federal
regulation.

As written, a City of Avalon Business License may only be suspended or revoked if a provision
of the business license chapter has been violated, the license has been granted on false or
fraudulent evidence, or the licensee has violated terms and conditions of the license.

With the current ordinance, if the licensee consistently violates other provisions of the AMC  —

compliance to the vehicle ordinance or parking regulations, participation in the City FOG
program, compliance with noise ordinance, etc. the business license cannot be revoked.
  —

By broadening the potential grounds for revocation and suspension, City Staff hope to see
greater compliance with other aspects of the AMCI as well as other state and federal regulations.

It should be noted, a suspension or revocation can only be processed if approved by the City
Council as outlined in AMC 3-1.116:
  —

  All matters pertaining to revocation or suspension shall be referred by the Director of
  Finance to the City Council. with a written statement of the reasons for the proposed
  revocation or suspension. The City Council shall give reasonable notice to the licensee
  to appear before the City Council at a time and place set for the hearing, to show cause
  why the license shall not be revoked or suspended. The notice shall state the grounds for
  the complaint or reasons for the proposed revocation or suspension in clear and concise
  language. The notice shall be sewed upon the licensee personally or by mail not less
  than 10 and not more than 20 days prior to the hearing date. At the hearing, the licensee
  shall be given the opportunity to appear personally or through counsel, to be heard, to
  defend the charges and to call witnesses. Upon good cause shown, the licensee shall be
   shall be given the opportunity to appear personally or through counsel, to be heard, to
  defend the charges and to call witnesses. Upon good cause shown, the licensee shall be
  entitled to a continuance until the next meeting of the City Council. After conducting such
  hearing, the City Council may revoke, suspend for a stated time period, or reinstate any
  license upon such terms and conditions as in the exercise of sound discretion is
  determined to be appropriate. The decision of the City Council shall be final and
  conclusive.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Undetermined.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The Avalon Municipal
Code will not be amended.

SUBJECT:  Avalon Wastewater Treatment Plant Soffit Repair and Chlorine
  Tank Replacement Procurement

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1 Make the affirmative finding that the City will not gain a
competitive advantage by using the formal contract bid or other competitive procedure as
outlined by the Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.111 (c); 2. Authorize the procurement of
supplies, equipment and services for the replacement and repair of the WVVTP soffit for a not to
exceed sum of $65,000; and 3. Authorize the procurement of supplies, equipment and services
for the replacement and repair of the WWTP chlorine tank for a not to exceed sum of $145,000.

REPORT SUMMARY:  The City’s wastewater treatment plant operator, PERC Water
Corporation (PERC), is completing major infrastructure repairs throughout the City’s Waste
Water Treatment Plant (WWTP), such as installation of a new screw press system as approved
by the City Council on October 17, 2023.

In addition to the establishment of new systems, PERC and City Staff are working to repair and
replace aging infrastructure. Two projects of significance include the repair and replacement of
a soffit located in the facility’s basement and the rehabilitation of the VVWTP’s chlorine contact
tank.

The soffit located in ceiling of the WWTP basement has spalled and delaminating concrete. The
existing condition is not safe and continued deterioration may further result in a future, more
costly repair as well as interfere with existing pump equipment located beneath the soffit. The
scope of work for this project includes chipping out all of the spalled concrete, replacing any
corroded rebar and then forming and repairing the concrete. The soffit repair and replacement
project is expected to cost approximately $65000.

The chlorine contact tank is a critical processing component within the WWTP. At the end of the
treatment process chlorine comes into contact with the processed wastewater within the chlorine
contact tank. Chlorine is the primary disinfectant used across the United States to reduce odor,
prevent algae growth, and remove iron and magnesium. The current tank has need of structural
repairs and features spalled and delaminated concrete. The scope of work mirrors the soffit
project including chipping out all of the spalled concrete, replacing any corroded rebar and then
forming and repairing the concrete. This project is expected to cost approximately $145000.

While the chlorine tank is being repaired, the processed wastewater flow will be treated through
a bypass. This diversion will allow Public Works and PERC crews the opportunity to repair and
replace valves within the tank as well as clean and repair the adjacent slide gate.
 Both projects are budgeted in FY 2023-24 and fall within the City’s Capital Improvement Plan  —

Capital Project #205012.

City Staff were made aware that a highly qualified contractor, Slater Waterproofing, Inc., that
specializes in this scope of work was currently on the Island performing work for a private entity.
Slater Waterproofing, Inc. is a reputable firm that has previously provided contractor services for
complex large-scale infrastructure projects for the City, including acting as the primary contractor
for the Cabrillo Mole Phase I Rehabilitation Project. SIster Waterproofing, Inc.’s experience,
  —

skill set, and the tact they are already mobilized and on the Island make them an ideal candidate
to perform the work needed at the WWTP.

With Slater Waterproofing, Inc. currently mobilized, and on Island, there will be a significant cost
savings for these two projects. City Staff have determined that the City will not gain a competitive
advantage by using the formal contract bid or other competitive procedure. Per Avalon Municipal
Code Section 3-4.111(c):

  If a competitive market does not exist, or the City wilt not gain a competitive advantage
  by using the format contract bid or other competitive procedure, or where the public
  project, goods or services may be obtained more economically or efficiently without the
  procedure, the City may dispense with format bidding or other competitive procedures.

Additionally, during the late fall and early winter months the WWTP’s process flow is greatly
reduced due to the reduced visitor counts. This time period is the best opportunity to complete
this scope of work. Staff recommends the City Council makes the affirmative finding that the City
will not gain a competitive advantage by using the formal contract bid or other competitive
procedure as outlined by the Avalon Municipal Code Section 3-4.111 (c) and authorize the
procurement of supplies, equipment and services for these projects.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Infrastructure reliability and safety.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Capital Project #205012 was approved by City Council in the 2023-24
budget and sufficient funding remains to implement the project

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The repair and
replacement of the aging infrastructure at the WWTP will not be completed in the most economic
and efficient way.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Direct City Staff to draft and execute agreements with Slater
Waterproofing Inc. for repair and replacement of the WWTP’s soffit and chlorine tank.

SUBJECT:  Authorize the Solicitation of a Request for Bids for the Five Corner
  Pedestrian Improvements Project

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): (1) Authorize the solicitation of a request for bids for the
construction contract for the Five Corner Intersection Enhancement and Safety Improvement
Project. (2) Approve the design and construction plans of the project. (3) Authorize the City
Manager or his designee to modify plans as needed for compliance with funding agencies.

REPORT SUMMARY: Since 2018, work has proceeded on developing the construction contract
documents to implement the reconstruction of the five corners intersection including the roadway
segments of Tremont Avenue and Avalon Canyon Road in the near vicinity of the intersection.
The project proposes to construct new permanent sidewalks, median safety islands, traffic
calming (mini-roundabouts) and lighting in order to provide safer operations for all users. The
total project is .25 miles in length.

Working with the City’s on call engineering firm ESG engineering, including traffic engineering
firm W-Trans, landscape architectural firm RRM and environmental planning firm Birdseye
Planning Group. a preliminary design was developed along with environmental studies and
compliance documents. Different methods were employed to receive public input including
surveys, community meetings, presentations to City Council and Planning Commission and a
live demonstration of the roundabout layouts. The environmental document is a Mitigated
Negative Declaration under CEQA, which was certified by the Planning Commission on August
21, 2019. The project was found to require no other permits.

The project was scheduled to go to construction in 2020 with above and underground utilities
being relocated in the first construction season in the fall of 2020. However, with the Covid-1 9
Pandemic causing logistically problems due to statewide shelter in place and also presenting
uncertain financial conditions the project construction was delayed.

To expedite the project, City Staff separated the utility phase from the total scope of the project
and developed a request for proposals for that specific scope of work. The RFP was circulated
for a period of approximately 4 weeks; however, only one bid was submitted by the stated
deadline. The submitted bid listed a total project cost that significantly exceeded the sum
anticipated. City Staff made the determination it would be more efficient and cost effective to bid
the project in total. To ensure that the project was fully funded the City applied for additional
 funding through the Active Transportation Program. The project was successful in receiving an
additional $3.8 million construction funding.

This project is primarily funded by grants including funds from Metro Local Transportation Funds,
via the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (Metro), State of California’s
State Active Transportation Grant via the California Transportation Commission (Cal-Trans), and
a local match from the City, primarily from City’s SB1 annual allocation from the state.

Simultaneously to submission of this project to the City Council, the project’s granting authorities
are reviewing the plans for compliance with the terms of funding. Staff anticipate minor revisions
to the submitted design plans, and request the City Council authorizes the City Manager or his
designee to modify plans as needed for compliance with Metro and Cal-Trans agencies.

At this time, staff anticipate authorization from Metro and Cal-Trans by December 2023. The
final project RFP will be circulated for review by the end of November. Bid results, financial
analysis and Staff recommendation on contract award is planned to go before the City Council
on in late January or early February, 2024.

The project plans are available at City Hall for review.
